Every transportation system has three components: rights-of-way, termini, and vehicles. For the auto transportation system public funding sources typically only pay for the maintenance of the rights-of-way (roads). Termini costs (parking) are usually paid for by developers who are required to meet min off-street parking standards and then lump the costs in with the ezped price of rent, goods, or services. Vehicle costs are then borne by individuals who buy personal autos. The cost of owning and operating the average car in Hawaii is about $9,000 per year, though this excludes most of the costs of parking which are bundled into other costs. In total, Oahu residents spend $6-8b/yr on their cars. Transit, on the other hand, always seems very expensive because cities have to pay for all three components upfront: guideways, stations, and trains. Yes, the rail project is expensive, but when you consider what Hawaii residents spend on transportation overall, the costs are not that big.

First is taxes.  If any of the investments are in taxable accounts than you will end up with less capital to reinvest after paying capital gains.  If you have been holding a particular stock for a considerable period this can be a big issue.  Say you have $10,000 of company A which is currently trading for twice what you bought it for.  That means a gain of $5,000, 1/2 of which is taxable.  So if your marginal rate is 40% than you have to pay $1,000 in tax.  That means the stock needs to decline more than 10% to make this cash positive.  That is a major correction, and while it does happen fairly often, timing has to be spot on to be on the right side of the trade.

Second is income.  Retired people frequently rely on the dividend income to fund there lifestyle.  If you are out of the market for any period of time, your income will be significantly lower.  Get the timing wrong and you will be on the losing side

Even a tiny country like Denmark uses the quartile method with a Hidiroglou-Bethelot transformation of price relatives. Proposals from StatCan methodologists to institute similar or more ambitious adjustment procedures in the Canadian CPI have always been rejected.
